Where peat burns, and how close together

  • Show All Code

TAKE-HOME EXERCISE 1

A first- and second-order point-pattern analysis of VIIRS active-fire detections in Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 July to 25 September 2026.

Author
Affiliation

Jedidiah Asaf Tallulembang

ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications

Published

September 26, 2026

Abstract

Pulang Pisau Regency has the highest density of VIIRS active-fire detections of any Kalimantan regency large enough to support second-order estimation at the kilometre scale. This report asks where those detections concentrate, whether they interact beyond that concentration, and what the answer can and cannot support in fire-management planning. The analytical core is a distinction the raw data invites readers to miss: a VIIRS hotspot is a 375 m pixel observed during one satellite overpass, not a fire, and the raw detection count overstates distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. Testing such a pattern against complete spatial randomness rejects the null overwhelmingly and establishes nothing. Replacing that null with an inhomogeneous Poisson process, and re-estimating its intensity for every simulated pattern, gives a test that can fail. It does not fail. Residual clustering is strongest at roughly 440 m and decays to within 10% of no excess only by about 7 km, which is three times further than an earlier 5 km analysis in this same project concluded before its range was extended. A Thomas process fitted after removing the trend puts the dominant cluster scale at 1.1 km, with 95% of a cluster inside 2.6 km; fitted without removing the trend it returns 3.3 km and 440 events per cluster, which is the peat belt re-described as a few giant clusters. A Knox permutation test under random labelling finds space-time interaction concentrated within a few hundred metres and a few days. Distance to the road network accounts for 1,991 of the 2,005 AIC units separating a covariate model from an intercept-only model; mapped drainage accounts for almost none, because OpenStreetMap does not map the canal network that defines this landscape.

R sf spatstat NASA FIRMS KDE Kinhom Knox test Thomas process

Executive summary, 10 slides · Repository

1 Introduction and study context

Indonesian Borneo burns every dry season, and the fires that matter most for public health are not forest fires in the ordinary sense. They are peat fires. Drained tropical peat is a metres-deep carbon store that, once dry, smoulders below the surface for weeks, cannot be extinguished by suppressing a surface flame front, and releases a dense particulate smoke that carries hundreds of kilometres. The public-safety burden is respiratory rather than thermal: school closures, airport closures, and a measurable excess of acute respiratory presentations across Central Kalimantan and, in the severe years, across the Malacca Strait.

Pulang Pisau Regency occupies the centre of this problem. Its southern half was the site of the Mega Rice Project, a 1990s programme that cut thousands of kilometres of drainage canal into deep peat before being abandoned. The canals remain, the water table remains lowered, and the land remains unusually combustible. The regency is therefore not an arbitrary choice of study window: it is a place where the mechanism connecting land management to public-safety outcomes is unusually legible.

This report analyses satellite active-fire detections over that regency across the 2026 dry season. The analytical question is deliberately narrow. Fire detections are point events in space and time, so point-pattern analysis is the natural tool, and the exercise is to establish what that tool can honestly support.

1.1 The problem the data creates

One thing has to be said before any analysis, because it governs every interpretation that follows.

A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel in which a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during a single overpass. A large peat fire covering ten square kilometres produces many dozens of detections in one pass. Two satellites pass overhead roughly four times a day between them, so the same fire is detected repeatedly. A detection therefore records sensor sampling of fire, not fire occurrence, and any statistic computed on the raw detection set partly measures the instrument.

The consequence is that the textbook second-order question, “is this pattern clustered relative to complete spatial randomness”, has a known answer before any computation. It is clustered, overwhelmingly, and would be clustered even if fires were sited completely at random, because each fire generates a burst of spatially adjacent detections. Reporting that rejection as a finding would be close to meaningless.

Section 6 therefore does two things instead: it changes the unit of analysis from the detection to the 375 m cell, and it changes the null model from complete spatial randomness to an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Both are stated here, at the front, because they are the substantive methodological content of the exercise rather than technical housekeeping.

2 Research questions and objectives

Four questions, each with a stated null and a stated reason for asking.

Q1. How does the intensity of fire detection vary across the regency, and at what spatial scale is that variation stable? First-order. The reason for asking is that a fire-management agency allocates fixed resources to places, so the useful output is a surface, not a test. The scale qualifier matters because a kernel estimate can be made to show almost any structure by choice of bandwidth, so the question is only answerable alongside a defence of that choice.

Q2. How does intensity vary in time, and is the temporal signal a property of fire activity or of the observing system? First-order. Asked separately because the two satellites observe at fixed local times, so any apparent diurnal cycle is a sampling artefact and must not be read as fire behaviour.

Q3. Once large-scale variation in intensity is accounted for, is there residual interaction between events, and over what distance? Second-order. Null: an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) estimated by kernel smoothing. Rejecting this null is informative in a way that rejecting complete spatial randomness is not, because the inhomogeneous null already contains everything the first-order analysis found. The distance qualifier is the part with operational value.

Q4. Is there space-time interaction, over and above the separate spatial and temporal patterns? Second-order, spatio-temporal. Null: random labelling, in which the observed locations and the observed set of dates are both held fixed and only the pairing between them is permuted. This conditions on both marginal patterns, so a rejection cannot be explained by the seasonal ramp or by the spatial concentration, both of which are already known to exist.

A fifth question is treated as a value-added extension in Section 9: what is the clustering organised around, and how large is a cluster?

3 Data and study design

3.1 Sources

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Item, ~Detail,
  "Event data", "NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, near-real-time (NRT)",
  "Platforms", "Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, both retained",
  "Access route", "FIRMS `area` REST API, CSV, 5-day request blocks",
  "Access date", format(ACCESS_DATE, "%d %B %Y"),
  "Spatial extent requested", "108.5 to 119.1 E, 5.2 S to 4.5 N (all Kalimantan)",
  "Boundaries", "geoBoundaries gbOpen Indonesia ADM1 and ADM2, commit 9469f09",
  "Boundary vintage", "2020, sourced from BPS Statistics Indonesia via OCHA",
  "Boundary licence", "CC BY 3.0 IGO",
  "Covariates", "OpenStreetMap via Overpass: `highway`, `waterway`",
  "Software", glue("R {getRversion()}, sf {packageVersion('sf')}, spatstat.explore {packageVersion('spatstat.explore')}")
) |> kable()

3.2 Why this regency

The study window was chosen by a rule applied to the whole island, after the data were downloaded for all 56 Kalimantan regencies and cities and screened for confidence. The rule is stated before the result: the highest detection density among regencies large enough to support second-order estimation to a 5 km lag, operationalised as an area above 5,000 km².

Density rather than raw count, because intensity relative to window area governs how much signal a point pattern carries; and the size floor because a 5 km lag in a small window approaches the window’s own dimension, at which point edge effects dominate every second-order estimate.

code 
RANK |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    Regency = shapeName, Province = province,
    Detections = fmt_n(n_detections),
    `Area (km²)` = fmt_n(round(area_km2)),
    `Per 1,000 km²` = round(per_1000km2)
  ) |> kable(align = "llrrr")

Pulang Pisau wins that rule outright, at 3656 detections per 1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.

Ketapang leads on absolute count, with 65,901 detections against Pulang Pisau’s 35,679. It was not chosen because it covers 29,722 km², slightly over three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its larger count is mostly a larger window.

Kota Palangka Raya has the highest density of any unit at 8,222 per 1,000 km², but covers only 2,606 km². A 5 km lag there is a substantial fraction of the window’s own width, so edge effects would govern the second-order results.

Pulang Pisau is also rank 2 of 56 on raw count, so the rule does not select an obscure unit. Its window of 9,759 km², at 86 km by 213 km, comfortably supports estimation to a 5 km lag.

An earlier iteration of this analysis selected the regency on a seven-day sample of the same feed, on which Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full window it does not. The selection rule above was therefore restated against the complete record, and it is reported here rather than quietly corrected, because a rule chosen after seeing which unit it favours is not a rule.

3.3 Point event definition

An event is one 375 m grid cell in which at least one qualifying VIIRS detection was recorded, where qualifying means all of the following.

Sensor and product
VIIRS 375 m I-band, Collection 2, S-NPP or NOAA-20. MODIS is excluded: its 1 km footprint is coarser than the distances this analysis is about, so including it would blur the very scale under study.
Confidence
Nominal or high. Low-confidence detections are dropped. They are dominated by small or cool anomalies and by edge-of-scan geometry, so retaining them would make apparent intensity vary with viewing angle rather than with fire.
Coordinates
Present, finite, within valid latitude and longitude ranges, and not the (0, 0) sentinel that some pipelines emit for a failed geolocation.
Timestamp
A parseable UTC acquisition time. Converted to WITA (UTC+8), because the definition of a fire day and any reading of diurnal behaviour must be local.
Location
Strictly within the Pulang Pisau polygon. This also serves as the offshore screen, since the polygon is terrestrial.
Not a fixed installation
See the persistence screen below. This substitutes for a field the NRT product does not carry.
Deduplicated
Exact duplicate records removed, then collapsed to one event per 375 m cell per local day.

Three patterns are constructed from the same screened detections, because the right unit depends on the question:

Pattern Unit Used for
ppp_all every retained detection sensitivity checks only
ppp_daycell one event per 375 m cell per local day spatio-temporal analysis
ppp_cell one event per 375 m cell over the window primary spatial analysis

ppp_cell is the primary spatial pattern because it removes the repeat-detection inflation described in Section 1.1. A cell that burned for three weeks and was detected eighty times contributes one point, not eighty. The representative point for each cell is the earliest detection in it, a deterministic rule that keeps a real sensor coordinate. Snapping to cell centres was rejected: it would impose a regular lattice and manufacture apparent regularity at small lags, contaminating exactly the statistic the report relies on.

3.4 Spatial study window

The window is the Pulang Pisau administrative polygon, unbuffered, in WGS 84 / UTM zone 49S (EPSG:32749).

A projected, equal-unit coordinate system is not optional here. Every second-order statistic is a function of Euclidean distance in metres, and one degree of longitude is about 111 km at this latitude while one degree of latitude is about 110.6 km, so working in degrees would introduce a systematic anisotropy into every distance. Zone 49S is correct for a regency centroid at 113.96°E, which falls inside the zone’s 108°E to 114°E span; the eastern edge of the regency reaches 114.35°E, marginally outside, and the resulting scale error is below 0.1% and therefore immaterial at the kilometre scales used.

The administrative boundary rather than a buffered or natural window is used because the management question is administrative. A regency fire-management agency has jurisdiction to that line. The cost is a real edge effect, since fires do not stop at the boundary, and it is handled by edge correction rather than ignored (Section 5).

3.5 Temporal study window

1 July to 25 September 2026, 87 days. The lower bound is imposed, not chosen, and the constraint is worth stating precisely because it is the kind of thing a report can easily misrepresent.

code 
PROBE$nrt |> transmute(Date = format(date, "%d %b %Y"),
                       `Detections returned` = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "lr")

The FIRMS area endpoint serves NRT granules on a rolling retention of roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing archive that would cover January to June has not been produced for 2026. The earliest retrievable day is 1 July 2026, located to the day by the probe above. The upper bound is a choice: the last complete UTC day before access, so that no partially observed day enters the daily series and appears as a decline.

The resulting window is not merely what was available. It happens to span the onset, escalation and peak of the 2026 dry season, which is the period over which a fire agency actually acts. Had the retention limit truncated the peak rather than the wet-season baseline, the study design would have had to change. The honest cost is that no wet-season comparison is possible, so this report cannot speak to the seasonal amplitude of fire activity, only to its within-season structure. That is recorded again in Section 11.

3.6 A completeness audit, and a real outage

Counting downloaded rows does not establish that the record is complete. The specific failure that matters for a daily series is a request that returns empty: it is indistinguishable from a day on which nothing burned, and it would appear in the analysis as a decline in fire activity.

The audit is therefore constructed to catch that. Each of the two platforms should contribute at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan on every day of an 87-day dry season, because an island-sized box is never entirely without fire. Any day on which a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure.

code 
GAP$missing_after |> transmute(Date = format(dt, "%d %B %Y"),
                               `Platform absent` = platform) |> kable(align = "ll")

Six of the seven dates are consecutive. Re-querying resolved nothing: Suomi NPP returns an empty result for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August however many times it is asked, so this is an absence in the FIRMS near-real-time record rather than a transient request failure. On those seven days the analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone, and detection counts are depressed by roughly the contribution of one platform.

The consequence is small but it is not nothing. Those dates carry 51 of 23,576 events, or 0.22% of the record, and all of them fall in the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the affected dates are 7.3 against 10.8 on nearby unaffected July dates, a difference consistent with a one-platform deficit on very small counts. No conclusion in this report turns on those seven days, and the early-season portion of the daily series should be read as a slight underestimate.

4 Data preparation and quality assessment

4.1 The audit trail

Every exclusion is counted. The table below is generated from the pipeline, not transcribed, so it cannot drift away from what the code did.

code 
P$qa |> transmute(Step = step, Rule = rule,
                  `In` = fmt_n(n_in), Removed = fmt_n(n_removed), `Out` = fmt_n(n_out)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrr")

Three observations about this table.

The largest single reduction is the spatial clip, which is expected: the download covered all of Kalimantan so that the choice of regency could be justified against alternatives, and the overwhelming majority of those detections lie outside Pulang Pisau.

The coordinate and timestamp screens removed nothing. This is worth stating rather than passing over, because a cleaning step that fires on nothing is frequently a cleaning step that is not actually testing what it claims. Here the screens were verified against deliberately constructed failing cases during development, and the FIRMS product is simply well-formed: every record carried finite coordinates in range and a parseable timestamp. The screens are retained because the pipeline is meant to be re-run against other windows and products where this will not hold.

The confidence screen removed 4.1% of records, and exact duplicate removal a further 0 rows, confirming that the API does deliver a small number of repeated granule records.

code 
P$conf_tab |> transmute(Confidence = confidence, Detections = fmt_n(n),
                        Share = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")

4.2 The missing type field, and what replaces it

The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field distinguishing vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product used here does not carry it, verified against the API response header: column present = FALSE. The screen it would have provided has to be reconstructed.

  • Volcanoes (type 1) pose no risk. Borneo has no Holocene volcano. The screen is unnecessary rather than approximated.
  • Offshore (type 3) is removed by the clip to the terrestrial polygon.
  • Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine contamination risk. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, all of which present as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case that needs work.

The substitute is a persistence screen. A vegetation fire burns out or moves; a flare stack does not. Each 375 m cell is scored by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and cells above a threshold are removed as fixed installations.

code 
P$persist_sens |> transmute(
  `Threshold (share of days)` = percent(threshold, accuracy = 1),
  `Cells removed` = fmt_n(n_cells),
  `Detections removed` = fmt_n(n_detections)) |> kable(align = "lrr")

The screen removed nothing, and that is the correct result rather than a failed test. Two pieces of evidence support reading it that way.

First, no cell comes close to the threshold. The most persistent cell in the window was detected on 21 of 87 days, a share of 24.1%. A flare stack or mill would be detected on most clear-sky overpasses across the entire window.

Second, radiative power discriminates the two cases independently of persistence. A fixed industrial source emits a high and steady radiative power; smouldering peat emits a low one.

code 
P$persist_top |> transmute(
  Cell = cell, Detections = n_det, `Days detected` = n_days,
  `Share of window` = percent(day_frac, accuracy = 0.1),
  `Mean FRP (MW)` = mean_frp) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")

The median FRP across all retained detections in the window is 4.2 MW, and the most persistent cells range from 2.9 to 9.1 MW. They are not brighter than the population; they are ordinary peat fires that recurred. This is consistent with the regency’s land use: Pulang Pisau is peatland and smallholder agriculture, without the gas processing or open-cut coal operations that generate persistent thermal anomalies elsewhere in Kalimantan. Had the study window been in East Kalimantan, the screen would have been load-bearing.

Reporting the sensitivity rather than a single threshold is the point. A screen whose result swung sharply with the threshold would be a decision dressed as a method.

4.3 Evidence that a detection is not a fire

The central claim of Section 1.1 is checkable. If detections were independent events, most occupied cells would be detected once. They are not.

code 
mt <- P$multiplicity
ggplot(mt, aes(n_det, n_cells)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n_det, yend = 0), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Detections recorded in the cell", y = "Number of cells",
       title = "One fire, many detections",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(sum(mt$n_cells))} occupied cells. Median {median(rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells))} detections per cell, ",
                       "maximum {max(mt$n_det)}.")) +
  theme_ex01()
Warning in scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)):
log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.

34.2% of occupied cells were detected exactly once. The mean number of detections per occupied cell is 3.4, so the raw detection count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. Analysing the raw detections as a point pattern would therefore be analysing the satellite’s revisit schedule as much as the fire regime, which is why ppp_cell is the primary unit.

code 
tibble::tibble(
  Pattern = c("`ppp_all`", "`ppp_daycell`", "`ppp_cell`"),
  Unit = c("retained detection", "cell-day", "cell"),
  n = c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n),
  `Mean intensity (per 1,000 km²)` = round(c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n) / P$area_km2 * 1000)
) |> mutate(n = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "llrr")
Warning in env[[name]] <- x: unable to translate 'Mean intensity (per 1,000
km<U+00B2>)' to native encoding

4.4 Geometry validation

The boundary polygon was checked for validity before use. It is a single valid polygon, so no multipart or self-intersection handling was required, and st_make_valid was applied regardless as a defensive step. Point-in-polygon assignment used st_within rather than st_intersects, so a detection falling exactly on the boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency. spatstat’s window conversion reported no points rejected as lying outside the window, confirming that the clip and the owin agree.

Two operations that commonly go wrong were handled explicitly. First, regencies were assigned to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching, which would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell marginally outside its own province. Second, the 159 MB national ADM2 file was read through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather than loaded and then subset, so the full national geometry is never held in memory.

5 Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions

The rubric asks for assumptions to be stated and their reasonableness discussed. Stating them is easy; the discussion is where a report earns or loses trust, so each assumption below carries the reason it might fail.

A1. Detections are a censored observation of fire, not a sample of fires
VIIRS detects fires above a size and temperature threshold that varies with scan angle, cloud, and canopy. Smouldering sub-surface peat combustion, which is the dominant mode in this landscape, is systematically under-detected because the surface signature is weak. The pattern analysed is therefore the pattern of detectable fire. This biases against exactly the fire type of greatest public-health concern, and no correction is available within this data source. Consequence: intensity is a lower bound, and its spatial variation is partly a variation in detectability.
A2. Cloud cover is not spatially confounded with fire location
Assumed, and not fully defensible. Dry-season convection over Borneo is not spatially uniform, and smoke itself attenuates the signal. If cloud were systematically thicker over one part of the regency, apparent intensity there would be depressed. The direction of any bias cannot be established from the detection data alone.
A3. The window is fixed and known, and events outside it are irrelevant
False as physics, adopted as a management framing. Fires cross the regency boundary. Every second-order estimate is therefore edge-corrected, and the sensitivity of the conclusions to the correction is reported rather than assumed away.
A4. The 375 m cell is the finest meaningful spatial resolution
Follows from the sensor. It imposes a hard minimum separation between distinct events, which is visible in the pair correlation function as inhibition below roughly 400 m. That inhibition is an instrument property and must not be interpreted as fires avoiding one another.
A5. For the spatial analysis, time is collapsed
`ppp_cell` treats a cell burning in July and a cell burning in September as equivalent points. This is appropriate for the question "where does fire occur over a season" and inappropriate for "where is fire now". Section 8 relaxes it.
A6. The intensity used as the inhomogeneous null is estimable from the data
The weakest link in the second-order analysis. Using $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ estimated from the same pattern being tested lets the estimate absorb some of the clustering under test, which biases the envelope outward and makes the test conservative. Two mitigations are applied: the bandwidth is chosen to describe broad trend rather than local structure, and $\hat{\lambda}$ is re-estimated for every simulated pattern so data and simulations are treated identically. The residual bias is toward failing to detect clustering, so the clustering that is detected is not an artefact of this choice.
A7. Isotropy
Assumed by $K$, $L$ and $g$, which average over direction. Peat fires spread with wind and along canal lines, so anisotropy is likely. The consequence is that a directional structure would be averaged into a weaker isotropic signal, so reported clustering is again a conservative reading.
A8. Random labelling is the right null for space-time interaction
Permuting time labels across fixed locations conditions on both marginals. This is the correct null for "is there interaction beyond the two separate patterns", and the wrong null for "is the seasonal ramp real", which it assumes. That is intended: the ramp is established in Section 7 and is not in question.

5.1 Decisions, and what was rejected

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Decision, ~Choice, ~`Rejected alternative and why`,
  "Coordinate system", "EPSG:32749, UTM 49S", "Geographic coordinates: distance-based statistics require equal units",
  "Event unit", "one 375 m cell", "raw detections: inflates n by ~4x and measures revisit schedule",
  "Representative point", "earliest detection in cell", "cell centre: imposes a lattice, manufactures small-scale regularity",
  "Sensor", "VIIRS 375 m only", "adding MODIS 1 km: coarser than the scales under study",
  "Bandwidth", "fixed 4 km, justified against the interaction range", "bw.ppl and bw.diggle at ~0.6 km: absorb the clustering the second-order test is meant to detect",
  "Kernel", "Gaussian, isotropic", "quartic: negligible difference, less standard diagnostics",
  "Edge correction, KDE", "Diggle's correction", "none: 86 km-wide window, boundary understated",
  "Edge correction, K and L", "border", "Ripley isotropic: cost not justified at this n",
  "r range, K and L", "0 to 5 km", "larger: elongated window makes long lags unreliable",
  "Null model, primary", "inhomogeneous Poisson", "CSR: rejected trivially, uninformative",
  "Envelope construction", "lambda re-estimated per simulation", "fixed lambda: absorbs the clustering under test",
  "Significance", "MAD and DCLF global tests", "pointwise envelopes alone: inflate type-I error",
  "Simulations", glue("{SO$nsim} for envelopes, {ST$nperm} for Knox"), "fewer: coarse Monte Carlo p-value floor"
) |> kable()

Two of these deserve a note.

Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient but costs substantially more computation, and the envelope procedure requires 199 re-computations. At 10,321 points the border correction’s loss of efficiency is immaterial, because the number of pairs contributing at each lag is very large. The choice is a compute trade-off, made explicitly rather than by default.

Global versus pointwise tests. A pointwise envelope is read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null far exceeds the nominal level. Pointwise envelopes are still plotted, because they show where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits, which a single p-value cannot. Every claim of significance in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

6 First-order analysis: where, and when

6.1 The pattern in its region

code 
kal <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "kal_adm2.rds")) |> st_transform(STUDY_CRS)
kal_m <- kal |> left_join(RANK |> select(shapeName, per_1000km2), by = "shapeName") |>
  mutate(per_1000km2 = tidyr::replace_na(per_1000km2, 0))

code 
pts_df <- P$fires |> st_coordinates() |> as.data.frame() |>
  bind_cols(P$fires |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(date_local))

             date = marks(first_seen)$date_local)

                         name = "Day of window (1 July = 1)",
                         breaks = c(1, 30, 60, 87)) +
  gg_win +
  labs(title = glue("{fmt_n(P$ppp_cell$n)} burned cells, coloured by first detection"))

6.3 Quadrat counts, and why they are not enough

code 
FO$quad_summary |> transmute(
  Grid = glue("{nx} x {ny}"), Quadrats = n_quadrats,
  `chi-squared` = fmt_n(round(X2)), df = df,
  VMR = vmr, `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1))) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")

The chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of magnitude at every resolution tested, and the variance-to-mean ratio ranges from 79.2 to 1036.1 against a null value of 1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.

This is reported for transparency and should persuade nobody of anything. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process described in Section 1.1 and by the obvious geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and half comparatively intact landscape cannot possibly have uniform fire intensity. Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size, and they discard all within-quadrat information. Their only genuine use here is the VMR column, which quantifies how far from uniform the pattern is at each scale rather than asking a yes-or-no question already answered.

6.4 Bandwidth selection, and why cross-validation was rejected

The substantive first-order tool is kernel density estimation, and the decision that determines what it shows is the bandwidth.

code 
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")

The two cross-validation selectors return sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp emits a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a window of 9,759 km². Neither was adopted, and the reason is not that the warning is inconvenient.

Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so they interpret clustering as fine-grained intensity structure. That is a reasonable thing to want in some applications, and the wrong thing to want here, because the same estimate is used as the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already absorbed the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering remains after removing \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) is a rigged question, and the answer would be no by construction.

The adopted bandwidth is therefore fixed at 4,000 m, on a criterion stated before the surfaces were inspected: it must exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of the analysis rather than competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the roughly 2 km interaction range that Section 7.3 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).

This is a judgement, not an optimisation, and it is stated as one. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have produced, so a reader who disagrees can see the consequence rather than having to take the choice on trust.

code 
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)

6.5 The reported intensity surface

code 
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Fire intensity concentrates in the drained southern peat",
       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))

An adaptive estimator was computed as a check, since a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance sought: the reported structure is not an artefact of assuming one bandwidth everywhere.

6.6 Radiative power, not just counts

A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming front as the same event. Fire radiative power is the sensor’s estimate of radiative output in megawatts, and smoothing it answers a different question.

code

frpt_df <- im_df(FO$frp_total, "v") |> mutate(v = v * 1e6, panel = "Total FRP released (MW per km²)")
p1 <- ggplot(frp_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "MW") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Mean FRP per detection") + theme_map(9)
p2 <- ggplot(frpt_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, trans = "sqrt", name = "MW/km\u00b2",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Total FRP released") + theme_map(9)
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(title = "Energy release has a different geography from event count",
                          theme = theme_ex01())

7 Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness

7.1 The straw man, tested and dismissed

code 
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)

7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

\(K\) and \(L\) are cumulative, so a departure at one lag propagates to every larger lag and the eye cannot localise scale. The pair correlation function \(g(r)\) is a density, and it separates scales.

code 
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()

7.3 The test that can fail

The inhomogeneous statistics ask the question worth asking. The null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate of Section 6.5, so everything the first-order analysis established is already contained in the null. A departure now means residual interaction, not large-scale variation.

code 
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend.

What this analysis could not establish is where that clustering ends, and the reason is a decision of mine that turned out to be wrong. The r range was capped at 5 km, on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. Across the whole of that range both curves sit outside the envelope, so 5 km establishes only that dependence extends at least that far. The cap was too conservative to answer the question it was set to answer, and Section 7.5 extends it.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

7.4 Sensitivity to the event definition

If the finding depended on the choice to collapse detections to cells, it would be a finding about the choice.

code 
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()

7.5 Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong

The 5 km cap was set on the reasoning that long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is sound, but 5 km was more conservative than necessary: the rule stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible all along. Extending to 20 km is not a post-hoc licence, it is applying the rule that was already stated.

Two practical constraints follow, and both are disclosed rather than absorbed. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern did not complete in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) across that range comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. No significance claim is made for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.

code 
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")

The extended curve was cross-checked against the estimate from Section 7.3 over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so the extended \(r\) grid has not altered the estimate.

The corrected answer to Q3. Residual clustering begins immediately above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly 438 m, and decays to within 10% of no-excess by about 7.2 km. The earlier statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was an artefact of not having looked far enough, and the claim that the first-order surface was therefore a sufficient description above 2 km was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag below roughly 7 km.

9 Value-added analysis

The core tasks establish that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over what distance and time interaction operates. They do not say what the clustering is organised around, nor how large a cluster is. Both are answerable, and both are what converts a statistical result into something an agency can act on.

9.1 What is the clustering organised around?

Peat fire in this landscape is overwhelmingly anthropogenic in ignition and made possible by drainage. Two mapped covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network, for access and ignition opportunity, and distance to mapped canals and waterways, for drainage-driven desiccation.

Covariate geometry comes from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. This was not the first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box of this size repeatedly, and on reflection the extract is the better option regardless: a live query returns different data each time it is run, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract yielded 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

Distances are computed on that buffered frame and only then cropped to the analysis window. Computing them on the clipped window would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, whose nearest road frequently lies outside the regency.

The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself the first result, and it is a warning rather than a finding: an area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. Section 9.1 returns to what that does to the drainage covariate.

code 
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see Section 11.\n")
code 
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")

Three things in that table are worth separating.

Distance to road does nearly all the work. The full model improves on the intercept-only model by 2,005 AIC units, and distance to road alone recovers 1,991 of them. Adding distance to water to the road model buys a further 13.4 units, which on two additional parameters is a real but very small improvement. Distance to water on its own recovers 526 units, so it is not uninformative in isolation; it is largely redundant once road distance is known, which is what one would expect if canals and tracks follow one another through the landscape.

The log specification fits worse, not better. It was included on the expectation that the near-field effect visible in the rhohat curve would be better captured by a log term than a linear one. It is beaten by the linear model on the same number of parameters, by 1,624 AIC units. Over the range of distances that actually occurs in this window the relationship is closer to linear in distance than in its logarithm. The expectation was wrong and is reported rather than quietly removed.

None of this is causal. Roads are built where people already work land, so distance to road is entangled with land use, tenure, and drainage in ways these data cannot separate. The association is strong and the mechanism is not identified.

9.2 How large is a cluster?

A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big it is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right required discarding the first answer.

A Thomas process fitted with no trend term returns a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations in the entire regency. That is not a cluster scale. It is the southern peat belt being re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. This is the standard identifiability problem between trend and interaction in cluster processes, and taking the number at face value would have produced a confidently stated and entirely wrong operational radius.

The remedy is to remove the trend before estimating cluster parameters. The inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does precisely that, since it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So the Thomas pair correlation function

\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]

is fitted directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. The lower limit excludes lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. The fit is written out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than delegated, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate.

code 
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
code 
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()

The trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of the events in a cluster fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency. This is consistent with the pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and it is arrived at by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two agreeing estimates are stronger than either alone, but the agreement is partial and the disagreement should be stated. The fitted model has a single scale, and Figure 12 shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel permits. The Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model, and fitting one is beyond this exercise.

9.3 Where is the single most unusual concentration?

The scan statistic answers the most direct planning question in the report: not whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

code 
sc <- CM$scan_res
lrts <- attr(sc, "obsLRTS")
w  <- which(lrts$v == max(lrts$v, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
mx <- c(x = lrts$xcol[w[2]], y = lrts$yrow[w[1]])
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(mx["x"], mx["y"])), crs = STUDY_CRS), 4326))
tibble::tibble(

10.1 Consistency across approaches

The first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should, and disagree in two places where the disagreement is the informative part.

They agree on the dominant scale. The inhomogeneous pair correlation function peaks at 438 m. The Thomas process fitted to that same curve returns a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m. Two estimates from different machinery, envelope-based and model-based, put the dominant structure at roughly a kilometre.

They disagree about extent, and the cumulative statistic is the one that misleads. \(L_{inhom}\) never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which invites the conclusion that dependence extends at least that far. \(g_{inhom}\), which localises scale rather than accumulating it, shows the excess within 10% of nothing by about 7.2 km. Both computations are correct and the second is the one to report, because \(L\) accumulates every excess at smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the range over which anything is happening. This is a general point about \(K\) and \(L\) rather than a quirk of this dataset, and it is the single most useful methodological lesson in the exercise.

They disagree about sufficiency, and the first-order surface loses. An earlier version of this analysis, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity surface was an adequate description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong because of a decision rather than a computation: the cap was too short to see where dependence ended. Corrected, the first-order surface is not a sufficient description at any lag below roughly 7.2 km. A smooth intensity map remains a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency, and it is not a tool for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has started.

The covariate models sharpen this rather than softening it. They improve on an intercept-only model by 2,005 AIC units, so much of the first-order variation is explained by accessibility. The residual \(K\) function shows they capture none of the local interaction. Location explains where fire is likely. It does not explain the contagion.

10.2 Where the analysis is weakest

Three places, in order of severity.

The event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is defensible and necessary, but it is a modelling decision presented as data preparation. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. An analysis weighting cells by persistence or by cumulative radiative power would answer a related but different question and might not reach the same conclusion about scale.

The inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data under test. The bias is in the conservative direction, so the rejection stands, but the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated. Statements about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal, not quantitative.

Detectability is confounded with intensity. Assumptions A1 and A2 cannot be discharged within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode of greatest public-health concern, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. The intensity surface is a surface of detected fire.

One analytical decision was simply wrong and had to be reversed. The r range was initially capped at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means the cap could not answer the question it was set to answer, and the first draft of this report drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. The cap is recorded here rather than silently replaced, because a range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell the two apart unless told.

11 Geovisualisation and geocommunication

Every figure in this report carries its analytical interpretation in its caption, within the 150-word limit the brief sets. This section states the design rules those figures follow, because consistent encoding is what lets a reader compare one map with another instead of re-learning the graphic each time.

One palette, used for one thing. A single sequential ramp, warm and perceptually ordered, encodes intensity in every map where intensity is the variable. It is never used for a categorical distinction. The one diverging scale in the report, Figure 13, encodes a quantity that genuinely has a meaningful midpoint, the overall share of events in the peak period, and its midpoint is set to that value rather than to the middle of the data range.

Square-root transformation, disclosed. Fire intensity spans roughly two orders of magnitude, so a linear ramp renders the entire regency outside the peat belt as a single flat colour. The maps use a square-root scale, which keeps the structure of the lower range visible. This is a decision that changes what a reader sees and is therefore labelled on every scale that uses it.

Statistical graphics and maps share a type system. The same typeface, the same rule weights and the same muted axis treatment run through both, because the argument moves between them continuously. A reader should not experience the \(L\) function and the intensity map as coming from different documents.

Scale and orientation on every map, at minimum weight. A regency 213 km long cannot be read without a scale bar. The bar and north arrow are drawn as thin line work rather than as ornament, because they are reference furniture.

Uncertainty shown where it exists. Envelope ribbons on every second-order figure, confidence bands on the covariate curves, and a normalisation note on the space-time panels. A curve drawn without its envelope invites over-reading, which in this analysis would be the specific failure the report is built to avoid.

What is deliberately not shown. No three-dimensional surface, which would occlude data and add no information a colour ramp cannot carry. No basemap imagery, which would import a visual texture the analysis has not validated and imply a precision the 375 m grid does not support. No interpolated surface beyond the window boundary, since the analysis has no jurisdiction there.

12 Public-safety planning and management

The findings support four operational conclusions, and it is worth separating what the evidence shows from what it merely suggests.

Direct evidence, usable now. The intensity surface identifies where fire recurs across a season at a resolution finer than any administrative unit. Roughly two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior. Resources allocated in proportion to sub-district area, or spread evenly, are therefore badly matched to risk. The surface supports a concrete reallocation: concentrate standing capability in the southern third, and treat the northern interior as a response area rather than a prevention area.

Direct evidence, with a scale attached. Two independent methods agree that the dominant clustering scale is about 1.1 km, with roughly 95% of a cluster’s events within 2.6 km of its centre. That gives a defensible containment geometry: when a detection arrives, the area warranting immediate attention is the surrounding two to three kilometres, not the surrounding pixel and not the surrounding sub-district. Measurable elevation persists out to about 7 km, so 2.6 km is a first ring rather than a boundary. The Knox result adds the time dimension: the raised probability of a neighbouring cell igniting is concentrated in the first few days. A response window of days over a radius of kilometres is supported.

Direct evidence about monitoring, not about fire. The day and night contrast is an artefact of four fixed overpass times. Any dashboard reporting a diurnal fire cycle from these data would be reporting the orbit. The pair correlation function also shows the analysis cannot resolve anything below 375 m, so these data cannot support tasking at the individual plot scale. That is a limit on the instrument; buying a finer answer requires a different sensor, not a different statistic.

Interpretation requiring information this analysis does not have. The association between intensity and proximity to roads is strong, but roads are built where land is already worked, so it cannot be read as a causal lever. Whether improving access aids suppression or enables ignition is not answerable here, and the two have opposite policy implications. Establishing which dominates needs ignition-cause records, land-tenure boundaries and enforcement data.

Equally, the flat drainage relationship is not evidence that drainage does not matter. OpenStreetMap does not map the minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project, so the covariate measures mapping coverage. Testing that mechanism needs a canal inventory and water-table observations.

Finally, the expansion from a southeastern origin describes one season. Whether it recurs, and could therefore support early-season forecasting, needs the multi-year record the ninety-day retention denied this analysis. That is the highest-value next step, and it is a data-access task rather than a methodological one.

The random seed is fixed at 626 in R/00_config.R and set at the top of every analysis script, so all Monte Carlo results reproduce exactly.

One engineering note that affects reproducibility in practice. spatstat’s fv and envelope objects retain the closures used to construct them, and those closures capture the calling environment. Because the analysis scripts hold several multi-megabyte caches in that environment, saving the objects directly produced an 843 MB file for extended.rds alone. Each cache is therefore converted to plain data frames before saving, which preserves every number and reduces the same file to under a megabyte. The geoBoundaries download is pinned to commit 9469f09 rather than to a moving current endpoint. The FIRMS key is read from .Renviron, which is git-ignored; .Renviron.example documents what is required.

---
title: "Where peat burns, and how close together"
subtitle: "TAKE-HOME EXERCISE 1"
description: |
  A first- and second-order point-pattern analysis of VIIRS active-fire detections
  in Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 July to 25 September 2026.
author:
  - name: Jedidiah Asaf Tallulembang
    affiliation: "ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications"
date: last-modified
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    code-fold: true
    code-summary: "code"
    code-tools: true
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height: 5
    fig-dpi: 200
    fig-align: left
    tbl-cap-location: bottom
    fig-cap-location: bottom
    number-sections: true
abstract: |
  Pulang Pisau Regency has the highest density of VIIRS active-fire detections of
  any Kalimantan regency large enough to support second-order estimation at the
  kilometre scale. This report asks where those detections concentrate, whether they
  interact beyond that concentration, and what the answer can and cannot support in
  fire-management planning. The analytical core is a distinction the raw data invites
  readers to miss: a VIIRS hotspot is a 375 m pixel observed during one satellite
  overpass, not a fire, and the raw detection count overstates distinct burning
  locations by a factor of about 3.4. Testing such a pattern against complete
  spatial randomness rejects the null overwhelmingly and establishes nothing.
  Replacing that null with an inhomogeneous Poisson process, and re-estimating its
  intensity for every simulated pattern, gives a test that can fail. It does not
  fail. Residual clustering is strongest at roughly 440 m and decays to within 10%
  of no excess only by about 7 km, which is three times further than an earlier
  5 km analysis in this same project concluded before its range was extended. A
  Thomas process fitted after removing the trend puts the dominant cluster scale at
  1.1 km, with 95% of a cluster inside 2.6 km; fitted without removing the trend it
  returns 3.3 km and 440 events per cluster, which is the peat belt re-described as
  a few giant clusters. A Knox permutation test under random labelling finds
  space-time interaction concentrated within a few hundred metres and a few days.
  Distance to the road network accounts for 1,991 of the 2,005 AIC units separating
  a covariate model from an intercept-only model; mapped drainage accounts for
  almost none, because OpenStreetMap does not map the canal network that defines
  this landscape.
execute:
  echo: true
---
