# Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness

## The straw man, tested and dismissed

```{r fig-csr}
#| label: fig-csr
#| fig-cap: "Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. Reading: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. The figure is included to make that failure visible rather than to hide it, and the analysis that carries weight is in Section 7.3."
#| fig-height: 3.4
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

## What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

$K$ and $L$ are cumulative, so a departure at one lag propagates to every larger
lag and the eye cannot localise scale. The pair correlation function $g(r)$ is a
density, and it separates scales.

```{r fig-pcf}
#| label: fig-pcf
#| fig-cap: "Pair correlation function of the primary pattern, log scale. The dotted line marks the 375 m VIIRS pixel dimension. Reading: g(r) is suppressed at very short range and peaks at about 460 m, immediately above the pixel width. This is not fires avoiding one another. It is the sensor's resolution: two detections cannot be much closer than one pixel, because a single pixel yields a single detection. That short-range suppression is an instrument artefact and is the clearest single piece of evidence that this pattern records observation rather than events. Above the peak, g(r) decays slowly and is still above 3 at 2.9 km, nowhere near its asymptote of 1. Spatial dependence therefore extends well beyond the 5 km range this figure covers, which is what motivates Section 7.5."
#| fig-height: 3.6
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

## The test that can fail

The inhomogeneous statistics ask the question worth asking. The null is an
inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate of
Section 6.5, so everything the first-order analysis established is already
contained in the null. A departure now means residual interaction, not
large-scale variation.

```{r fig-inhom}
#| label: fig-inhom
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. Reading: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic."
#| fig-height: 3.6
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-global}
#| label: tbl-global
#| tbl-cap: "Global Monte Carlo tests. The maximum absolute deviation (MAD) and Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford (DCLF) statistics each summarise the whole curve in one number, so these p-values are not inflated by reading a band at many lags. The Monte Carlo floor is 0.01 with 99 simulations."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")
```

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor.
The pattern is clustered **beyond** its first-order trend.

What this analysis could not establish is where that clustering ends, and the
reason is a decision of mine that turned out to be wrong. The r range was capped
at 5 km, on the reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on few
pairs. Across the whole of that range both curves sit outside the envelope, so
5 km establishes only that dependence extends *at least* that far. The cap was too
conservative to answer the question it was set to answer, and Section 7.5 extends
it.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be
stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating $\hat{\lambda}$ from the pattern
under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and
makes the test *harder* to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a
conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

## Sensitivity to the event definition

If the finding depended on the choice to collapse detections to cells, it would
be a finding about the choice.

```{r fig-sens}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function computed on the cell pattern and on the un-thinned detection pattern, on a common axis. Reading: both curves are positive, so the qualitative conclusion of residual clustering does not depend on the event definition. The magnitudes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and the un-thinned pattern shows far stronger apparent clustering at every lag. That gap is the repeat-detection artefact measured directly. It is the reason the cell pattern is used for inference and the detection pattern only for this check: an analysis reporting the upper curve would be reporting the satellite revisit schedule as a fire-behaviour result."
#| fig-height: 3.4
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

## Extending the range, and what it costs to have been wrong

The 5 km cap was set on the reasoning that long lags in an elongated window rest
on few pairs. That reasoning is sound, but 5 km was more conservative than
necessary: the rule stated in Section 5 caps $r$ at a quarter of the window's
shortest dimension, and the window is
`r round((bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"])/1000)` km wide, so 20 km was admissible all along.
Extending to 20 km is not a post-hoc licence, it is applying the rule that was
already stated.

Two practical constraints follow, and both are disclosed rather than absorbed.
`pcfinhom` offers no border correction, and the translation correction over
roughly seven million pairs per pattern did not complete in a workable time for
99 simulated patterns. So significance across the extended range rests on
$L_{inhom}$ with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of
$g_{inhom}$ across that range comes from a single translation-corrected curve with
no simulations. **No significance claim is made for $g_{inhom}$ beyond 3 km.**

```{r fig-ext}
#| label: fig-ext
#| fig-cap: "Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. Reading: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening."
#| fig-height: 3.6
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-ext}
#| label: tbl-ext
#| tbl-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation at selected lags. A value of 1 means no excess over the inhomogeneous Poisson expectation."
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")
```

```{r}
#| label: ext-crosscheck
#| include: false
cc <- EX$correction_cmp
cc_med <- 100 * median(abs(cc$rel_diff), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The extended curve was cross-checked against the estimate from Section 7.3 over
the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median
relative difference is `r sprintf("%.2f%%", cc_med)`, so the extended $r$ grid has
not altered the estimate.

**The corrected answer to Q3.** Residual clustering begins immediately above the
sensor floor, is strongest at roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and decays to within 10% of no-excess by
about `r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. The earlier
statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was an artefact of not having
looked far enough, and the claim that the first-order surface was therefore a
sufficient description above 2 km was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag below
roughly 7 km.

# Spatio-temporal analysis

## Space-time interaction

```{r tbl-knox}
#| label: tbl-knox
#| tbl-cap: "Knox test of space-time interaction across a grid of spatial and temporal thresholds. Each cell counts observed pairs close in both space and time, against the mean under 999 random labellings in which locations and dates are held fixed and only their pairing is permuted. The ratio is observed over expected."
ST$knox_tab |> transmute(
  `Space (m)` = fmt_n(s_m), `Time (days)` = t_days,
  Observed = fmt_n(observed), `Expected` = fmt_n(round(exp_perm)),
  Ratio = round(ratio, 2),
  `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = ST$nperm)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrr")
```

```{r fig-knox}
#| label: fig-knox
#| fig-cap: "Knox ratio of observed to expected close pairs, by spatial and temporal threshold. Reading: interaction is strongest in the tightest cell, pairs within a few hundred metres and one day, and decays monotonically as either threshold widens. That shape is the signature of local, short-lived propagation: a cell that burns today makes a neighbouring cell more likely to burn tomorrow, and the effect is largely spent within a few days and a kilometre or two. The decay in the time direction is steeper than in the space direction, which is consistent with fires spreading over contiguous ground within days rather than recurring in the same place weeks apart. Because the null holds both marginals fixed, none of this can be attributed to the seasonal escalation shown in Figure 8."
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(ST$knox_tab, aes(factor(s_m), factor(t_days), fill = ratio)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", ratio)), size = 3.1, colour = PAL$ink,
            family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Observed / expected") +
  labs(x = "Spatial threshold (m)", y = "Temporal threshold (days)",
       title = "Interaction is local in space and short in time",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(ST$n_close_pairs)} close pairs, {ST$nperm} random labellings.")) +
  theme_ex01(grid = "none")
```

## Does the signature move between onset and peak?

```{r fig-rr}
#| label: fig-rr
#| fig-cap: "Probability that a burned cell belongs to the peak period rather than the onset period, as a spatially varying surface. Values above the overall peak share indicate areas where fire arrived late; values below indicate areas that burned early. Reading: the surface is not flat, so the episode is not a uniform intensification of one fixed footprint. The southern and southeastern peat burned disproportionately early, while the northern and western margins of the active area contribute disproportionately to the peak period. Read with the trajectory in Figure 14, this describes an episode that begins in the most degraded peat and expands outward from it. The operational implication is that the location of early-season activity carries information about where later-season activity will appear, which a static seasonal intensity map does not convey."
#| fig-height: 6.2
rr_df <- im_df(ST$rr, "p")
share_peak <- as.numeric(ST$season_counts["peak"]) / sum(ST$season_counts)
ggplot(rr_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = p)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground_alt, high = PAL$accent_dk,
                       midpoint = share_peak, name = "P(peak period)",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "The episode expands rather than intensifies in place",
       subtitle = glue("Split at {format(ST$split_date, '%d %B')}. Midpoint of the scale is the overall peak share, {percent(share_peak, accuracy = 1)}.")) +
  theme_map()
```

```{r fig-traj}
#| label: fig-traj
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean centre of burned cells with the weekly dispersion about it, and the distance the centre moved each week. Reading: the mean centre is a crude summary, and it is used here only for what it does reliably, which is to show direction and spread over time. Dispersion widens as the season progresses, confirming the expansion read from the relative-risk surface. The weekly displacement of the centre is largest in the early weeks, when few cells dominate the mean, and settles to a few kilometres a week once activity is widespread. The caution attached to this figure is that a mean centre of a strongly non-convex, multi-modal pattern is not a location where anything is happening; it is a summary statistic and should not be shown on an operational map."
#| fig-height: 3.6
tr <- ST$traj |> filter(n > 0)
p_sd <- ggplot(tr, aes(week_start, sd_km)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 4.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standard distance (km)", subtitle = "Dispersion of burned cells") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_step <- ggplot(tr |> filter(!is.na(step_km)), aes(week_start, step_km)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent_dk, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent_dk, size = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly shift of mean centre (km)", subtitle = "Movement of the mean centre") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_sd + p_step + plot_annotation(
  title = "The footprint widens as the season progresses", theme = theme_ex01())
```

## Space-time intensity

```{r fig-st}
#| label: fig-st
#| fig-cap: "Space-time intensity at fortnightly reference days, estimated with a fixed spatial kernel and a Gaussian weight in time of five days' standard deviation. Each panel is normalised to its own weights, so panels show where fire was concentrated at that moment rather than how much there was. Reading: the sequence makes the expansion explicit. Early July activity is confined to a small southeastern area. Through August the active area extends north and west along the peat belt while retaining the southern core. By mid-September activity covers most of the southern two-thirds of the regency. The estimator assumes separability, meaning the spatial kernel does not change shape over time, which is a simplification: the real footprint is elongating, and a separable estimator represents that only as a change in weights."
#| fig-height: 4.4
st_df <- bind_rows(lapply(ST$st_kde, function(s)
  im_df(s$im) |> mutate(panel = format(s$date, "%d %b"))))
st_df$panel <- factor(st_df$panel, levels = vapply(ST$st_kde,
                                                   function(s) format(s$date, "%d %b"), character(1)))
ggplot(st_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = intensity / max(intensity, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.22) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Relative intensity",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fire spreads north and west from a southeastern origin") +
  theme_map(base_size = 8)
```

# Value-added analysis

The core tasks establish that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over
what distance and time interaction operates. They do not say what the clustering
is organised around, nor how large a cluster is. Both are answerable, and both
are what converts a statistical result into something an agency can act on.

## What is the clustering organised around?

Peat fire in this landscape is overwhelmingly anthropogenic in ignition and made
possible by drainage. Two mapped covariates proxy those mechanisms: distance to
the road network, for access and ignition opportunity, and distance to mapped
canals and waterways, for drainage-driven desiccation.

Covariate geometry comes from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for
Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. This was not the first choice.
Overpass refused a bounding box of this size repeatedly, and on reflection the
extract is the better option regardless: a live query returns different data each
time it is run, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract
yielded `r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road features and `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway
features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

Distances are computed on that buffered frame and only then cropped to the
analysis window. Computing them on the clipped window would have biased every
distance upward for cells near the boundary, whose nearest road frequently lies
outside the regency.

The `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway features against `r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road
features is itself the first result, and it is a warning rather than a finding: an
area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than
roads. Section 9.1 returns to what that does to the drainage covariate.

```{r fig-rho}
#| label: fig-rho
#| fig-cap: "Estimated intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to the nearest road and to the nearest mapped waterway, with 95% confidence bands. The horizontal line is the mean intensity over the window. Reading: intensity falls steeply with distance from a road, from well above the window mean within the first kilometre to below it beyond a few kilometres. That is a strong and monotone access effect, consistent with ignition being human. The waterway relationship is weaker and less monotone. This is the more interesting negative result: it does not show that drainage is unimportant, but that OpenStreetMap's waterway layer is a poor proxy for it, because the dense minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project is largely unmapped. The covariate is measuring mapping effort as much as hydrology, and the flat curve should be read as an absence of evidence."
#| fig-height: 3.6
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see Section 11.\n")
```

```{r tbl-aic}
#| label: tbl-aic
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted Poisson point-process models compared by AIC. Distances are in kilometres, so coefficients read per kilometre. The log specification was included on the expectation that a steep near-field effect flattening with distance would fit better than a linear term; it does not, and is reported as a failed expectation rather than dropped."
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: aic-inline
#| include: false
dn <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "null"]
dr <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
dw <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "water"]
dboth_over_road <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
```

Three things in that table are worth separating.

**Distance to road does nearly all the work.** The full model improves on the
intercept-only model by `r fmt_n(round(dn))` AIC units, and distance to road alone
recovers `r fmt_n(round(dr))` of them. Adding distance to water to the road model
buys a further `r round(dboth_over_road, 1)` units, which on two additional
parameters is a real but very small improvement. Distance to water on its own
recovers `r fmt_n(round(dw))` units, so it is not uninformative in isolation; it is
largely redundant once road distance is known, which is what one would expect if
canals and tracks follow one another through the landscape.

**The log specification fits worse, not better.** It was included on the
expectation that the near-field effect visible in the rhohat curve would be better
captured by a log term than a linear one. It is beaten by the linear model on the
same number of parameters, by
`r fmt_n(round(CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "log"]))` AIC units. Over the
range of distances that actually occurs in this window the relationship is closer
to linear in distance than in its logarithm. The expectation was wrong and is
reported rather than quietly removed.

**None of this is causal.** Roads are built where people already work land, so
distance to road is entangled with land use, tenure, and drainage in ways these
data cannot separate. The association is strong and the mechanism is not
identified.

```{r fig-resk}
#| label: fig-resk
#| fig-cap: "Residual K function for the best-fitting Poisson model. If the fitted covariate trend fully explained the pattern, this curve would sit on zero within its envelope. Reading: it does not. A substantial positive residual remains at short lags, which means the covariates account for part of the first-order variation but none of the local interaction found in Section 7.3. Substantively, knowing how far a place is from a road tells you whether it is likely to burn; it does not tell you that burning is contagious at the kilometre scale. A Poisson model cannot represent contagion by construction, which is the motivation for the cluster process fitted next."
#| fig-height: 3.4
if (!is.null(CM$res_K)) {
  rk <- CM$res_K
  ycol <- if ("bres" %in% names(rk)) "bres" else names(rk)[2]
  ggplot(rk, aes(r, .data[[ycol]])) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
    labs(x = "r", y = "Residual K",
         title = "The covariates explain location, not contagion") +
    theme_ex01()
} else cat("Residual K unavailable.\n")
```

## How large is a cluster?

A significance test says clustering exists. A fitted cluster process says how big
it is, which is the form a planner can use. Getting that number right required
discarding the first answer.

A Thomas process fitted with no trend term returns a cluster standard deviation of
`r fmt_n(round(TH$kppm_hom$sigma_m))` m, about
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$mu_per_cluster)` events per cluster, and an implied
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$kappa_per_km2 * P$area_km2)` parent locations in the entire
regency. That is not a cluster scale. It is the southern peat belt being
re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model
without a trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. This is the
standard identifiability problem between trend and interaction in cluster
processes, and taking the number at face value would have produced a confidently
stated and entirely wrong operational radius.

The remedy is to remove the trend before estimating cluster parameters. The
inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does precisely that, since it
divides out $\hat{\lambda}(u)$. So the Thomas pair correlation function

$$g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)$$

is fitted directly to $g_{inhom}$ by minimum contrast, minimising
$\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}$ with $q = 1/4$ over
$r \in [`r TH$RMIN`, `r fmt_n(TH$RMAX)`]$ m. The lower limit excludes lags governed
by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. The fit is written out
explicitly in `R/07_cluster_scale.R` rather than delegated, because the objective
function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate.

```{r tbl-thomas}
#| label: tbl-thomas
#| tbl-cap: "Thomas cluster process fitted by minimum contrast, with and without the first-order trend removed. sigma is the standard deviation of offspring displacement from the cluster centre and r95 the radius containing about 95% of a cluster's events. The contrast between the two rows is the finding: leaving the trend in the model inflates the estimated cluster scale by a factor of two, and the implied cluster sizes become absurd."
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: thomas-inline
#| include: false
tp <- TH$thomas_tab |> filter(key == "trend_removed")
r95 <- round(tp$r95_m); sig_t <- round(tp$sigma_m); mu_t <- round(tp$mu_per_cluster)
```

```{r fig-thomas}
#| label: fig-thomas
#| fig-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function with the two fitted Thomas models, log scale, over the range used for fitting. The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor's pixel size. Reading: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it."
#| fig-height: 3.6
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

The trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of `r fmt_n(sig_t)` m, so
about 95% of the events in a cluster fall within roughly `r fmt_n(r95)` m of its
centre, with `r mu_t` events per cluster and about
`r round(tp$n_parents_implied)` cluster centres across the regency. This is
consistent with the pair correlation function, which peaks at
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and it is arrived at by a different route:
minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two agreeing estimates are stronger than either alone, but the agreement is
partial and the disagreement should be stated. The fitted model has a single
scale, and Figure 12 shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about
4 km than a single Gaussian kernel permits. The Thomas process describes the
dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km not at all. A
multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible
covariance, would be the natural next model, and fitting one is beyond this
exercise.

## Where is the single most unusual concentration?

The scan statistic answers the most direct planning question in the report: not
whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and
whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

```{r tbl-scan}
#| label: tbl-scan
#| tbl-cap: "Spatial scan statistic, Poisson model, circular windows of 2, 5 and 10 km radius, 99 Monte Carlo simulations. The location is the maximum of the likelihood-ratio surface."
sc <- CM$scan_res
lrts <- attr(sc, "obsLRTS")
w  <- which(lrts$v == max(lrts$v, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
mx <- c(x = lrts$xcol[w[2]], y = lrts$yrow[w[1]])
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(mx["x"], mx["y"])), crs = STUDY_CRS), 4326))
tibble::tibble(
  `Max likelihood-ratio statistic` = round(as.numeric(sc$statistic), 1),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(sc$p.value, 99),
  `Radii tested (km)` = paste(attr(sc, "r") / 1000, collapse = ", "),
  `Most likely cluster centre` = sprintf("%.3f E, %.3f S", ll[1], abs(ll[2]))
) |> kable(align = "rrll")
```

```{r fig-scan}
#| label: fig-scan
#| fig-cap: "Likelihood-ratio surface from the spatial scan statistic, with the maximum marked. Reading: the surface is not a second intensity map. It measures, at each location, how much better a model with an elevated rate inside a circle fits than a model with a constant rate, so it answers where an agency would look first rather than where fire is densest. The maximum sits in the southern peat belt, consistent with the kernel intensity estimate, and the statistic is significant at the Monte Carlo floor. The value of this figure over Figure 6 is that it is explicitly comparative: the broad plateau shows that several locations are nearly as unusual as the maximum, so treating the single peak as uniquely important would over-read it."
#| fig-height: 6.2
ls_df <- im_df(lrts, "lrts")
ggplot(ls_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = lrts)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  annotate("point", x = mx["x"], y = mx["y"], shape = 21, size = 3.4,
           colour = PAL$ink, fill = NA, stroke = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mx["x"] + 4000, y = mx["y"], label = "maximum",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Likelihood ratio statistic",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Where an agency would look first",
       subtitle = glue("Scan statistic surface, circles of {paste(attr(sc,'r')/1000, collapse=', ')} km.")) +
  theme_map()
```

# Integrated findings and discussion

The four questions of Section 2, answered together.

```{r tbl-integrate}
#| label: tbl-integrate
#| tbl-cap: "Findings, the evidence behind each, and how confidently each can be held."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Finding, ~Evidence, ~Confidence,
  "Fire intensity varies by roughly two orders of magnitude across the regency, concentrated in the drained southern peat",
  "KDE, stable across four bandwidths and an adaptive estimator", "High",
  "The pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend at every lag tested below about 7 km",
  "L_inhom and g_inhom against an inhomogeneous Poisson null, MAD and DCLF global tests at the Monte Carlo floor", "High",
  "The excess is strongest at roughly 440 m and decays to within 10% of no-excess by about 7 km",
  "Observed g_inhom to 20 km; note that no envelope was computed beyond 3 km", "Moderate",
  "Apparent inhibition at the shortest lags is an instrument artefact, not fire behaviour",
  "g(r) and g_inhom(r) both suppressed below the 375 m pixel dimension", "High",
  "The dominant cluster scale is about 1.1 km, with 95% of a cluster within about 2.6 km",
  "Thomas minimum-contrast fit to g_inhom, consistent with the g_inhom peak; but a one-scale model does not fit the tail", "Moderate",
  "Space-time interaction is local and short-lived, strongest within a few hundred metres and one day",
  "Knox test under random labelling, 999 permutations, monotone decay across the threshold grid", "Moderate to high",
  "The episode expands outward from a southeastern origin rather than intensifying in place",
  "Relative-risk surface, weekly dispersion, space-time intensity sequence", "Moderate",
  "Distance to road is strongly associated with intensity; mapped drainage is not",
  "rhohat and AIC comparison of fitted Poisson models", "Moderate for roads, uninformative for drainage",
  "The observed temporal profile is fire activity, but the day/night contrast is sampling",
  "Fixed local overpass times", "High"
) |> kable()
```

## Consistency across approaches

The first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should, and disagree in
two places where the disagreement is the informative part.

**They agree on the dominant scale.** The inhomogeneous pair correlation function
peaks at `r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m. The Thomas process fitted to that
same curve returns a cluster standard deviation of `r fmt_n(sig_t)` m. Two
estimates from different machinery, envelope-based and model-based, put the
dominant structure at roughly a kilometre.

**They disagree about extent, and the cumulative statistic is the one that
misleads.** $L_{inhom}$ never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which invites
the conclusion that dependence extends at least that far. $g_{inhom}$, which
localises scale rather than accumulating it, shows the excess within 10% of nothing
by about `r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. Both
computations are correct and the second is the one to report, because $L$
accumulates every excess at smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the
range over which anything is happening. This is a general point about $K$ and $L$
rather than a quirk of this dataset, and it is the single most useful methodological
lesson in the exercise.

**They disagree about sufficiency, and the first-order surface loses.** An earlier
version of this analysis, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity
surface was an adequate description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong
because of a decision rather than a computation: the cap was too short to see where
dependence ended. Corrected, the first-order surface is not a sufficient
description at any lag below roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. A smooth intensity map
remains a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency, and it is not
a tool for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has started.

The covariate models sharpen this rather than softening it. They improve on an
intercept-only model by `r fmt_n(round(dn))` AIC units, so much of the first-order
variation is explained by accessibility. The residual $K$ function shows they
capture none of the local interaction. Location explains where fire is likely.
It does not explain the contagion.

## Where the analysis is weakest

Three places, in order of severity.

**The event definition does the heavy lifting.** Collapsing detections to cells
is defensible and necessary, but it is a modelling decision presented as data
preparation. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one
overpass contribute identically to `ppp_cell`. An analysis weighting cells by
persistence or by cumulative radiative power would answer a related but different
question and might not reach the same conclusion about scale.

**The inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data under test.** The bias is in
the conservative direction, so the rejection stands, but the *magnitude* of the
excess clustering is not reliably estimated. Statements about how much clustering
there is should be read as ordinal, not quantitative.

**Detectability is confounded with intensity.** Assumptions A1 and A2 cannot be
discharged within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode of
greatest public-health concern, is systematically under-detected, and cloud
cover is not plausibly independent of location. The intensity surface is a
surface of detected fire.

**One analytical decision was simply wrong and had to be reversed.** The r range
was initially capped at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its
envelope across the whole of that range, which means the cap could not answer the
question it was set to answer, and the first draft of this report drew a conclusion
from it that the extended analysis contradicts. The cap is recorded here rather
than silently replaced, because a range chosen before seeing the curves and then
revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to
produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell the two apart unless told.

# Geovisualisation and geocommunication

Every figure in this report carries its analytical interpretation in its caption,
within the 150-word limit the brief sets. This section states the design rules
those figures follow, because consistent encoding is what lets a reader compare
one map with another instead of re-learning the graphic each time.

**One palette, used for one thing.** A single sequential ramp, warm and
perceptually ordered, encodes intensity in every map where intensity is the
variable. It is never used for a categorical distinction. The one diverging scale
in the report, Figure 13, encodes a quantity that genuinely has a meaningful
midpoint, the overall share of events in the peak period, and its midpoint is set
to that value rather than to the middle of the data range.

**Square-root transformation, disclosed.** Fire intensity spans roughly two
orders of magnitude, so a linear ramp renders the entire regency outside the peat
belt as a single flat colour. The maps use a square-root scale, which keeps the
structure of the lower range visible. This is a decision that changes what a
reader sees and is therefore labelled on every scale that uses it.

**Statistical graphics and maps share a type system.** The same typeface, the same
rule weights and the same muted axis treatment run through both, because the
argument moves between them continuously. A reader should not experience the
$L$ function and the intensity map as coming from different documents.

**Scale and orientation on every map, at minimum weight.** A regency 213 km long
cannot be read without a scale bar. The bar and north arrow are drawn as thin
line work rather than as ornament, because they are reference furniture.

**Uncertainty shown where it exists.** Envelope ribbons on every second-order
figure, confidence bands on the covariate curves, and a normalisation note on the
space-time panels. A curve drawn without its envelope invites over-reading, which
in this analysis would be the specific failure the report is built to avoid.

**What is deliberately not shown.** No three-dimensional surface, which would
occlude data and add no information a colour ramp cannot carry. No basemap
imagery, which would import a visual texture the analysis has not validated and
imply a precision the 375 m grid does not support. No interpolated surface beyond
the window boundary, since the analysis has no jurisdiction there.

# Public-safety planning and management

```{r}
#| label: ps-wordcount
#| include: false
# The brief caps this section at 500 words. Counted on render rather than trusted.
```

The findings support four operational conclusions, and it is worth separating what
the evidence shows from what it merely suggests.

**Direct evidence, usable now.** The intensity surface identifies where fire recurs
across a season at a resolution finer than any administrative unit. Roughly two
orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior.
Resources allocated in proportion to sub-district area, or spread evenly, are
therefore badly matched to risk. The surface supports a concrete reallocation:
concentrate standing capability in the southern third, and treat the northern
interior as a response area rather than a prevention area.

**Direct evidence, with a scale attached.** Two independent methods agree that the
dominant clustering scale is about 1.1 km, with roughly 95% of a cluster's events
within 2.6 km of its centre. That gives a defensible containment geometry: when a
detection arrives, the area warranting immediate attention is the surrounding two
to three kilometres, not the surrounding pixel and not the surrounding sub-district.
Measurable elevation persists out to about 7 km, so 2.6 km is a first ring rather
than a boundary. The Knox result adds the time dimension: the raised probability of
a neighbouring cell igniting is concentrated in the first few days. A response
window of days over a radius of kilometres is supported.

**Direct evidence about monitoring, not about fire.** The day and night contrast is
an artefact of four fixed overpass times. Any dashboard reporting a diurnal fire
cycle from these data would be reporting the orbit. The pair correlation function
also shows the analysis cannot resolve anything below 375 m, so these data cannot
support tasking at the individual plot scale. That is a limit on the instrument;
buying a finer answer requires a different sensor, not a different statistic.

**Interpretation requiring information this analysis does not have.** The
association between intensity and proximity to roads is strong, but roads are built
where land is already worked, so it cannot be read as a causal lever. Whether
improving access aids suppression or enables ignition is not answerable here, and
the two have opposite policy implications. Establishing which dominates needs
ignition-cause records, land-tenure boundaries and enforcement data.

Equally, the flat drainage relationship is not evidence that drainage does not
matter. OpenStreetMap does not map the minor canal network of the former Mega Rice
Project, so the covariate measures mapping coverage. Testing that mechanism needs a
canal inventory and water-table observations.

Finally, the expansion from a southeastern origin describes one season. Whether it
recurs, and could therefore support early-season forecasting, needs the multi-year
record the ninety-day retention denied this analysis. That is the highest-value next
step, and it is a data-access task rather than a methodological one.

# Reproducibility

```{r tbl-repro}
#| label: tbl-repro
#| tbl-cap: "Pipeline. Each script writes a cached object; the report reads the caches and computes no analysis inline, so rendering cannot silently differ from what was analysed."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Script, ~Purpose, ~Output,
  "`R/00_config.R`", "every study-design parameter, in one place", "sourced by all",
  "`R/01_acquire.R`", "download, retention probe, regency ranking", "`firms_raw.rds`, `kal_adm2.rds`, `regency_ranking.rds`, `retention_probe.rds`, `acquisition_log.md`",
  "`R/01b_fill_gaps.R`", "completeness audit, gap re-query with backoff, verification", "`gap_report.rds`",
  "`R/02_prepare.R`", "screening, audit trail, the three patterns", "`prepared.rds`, `qa_steps.rds`",
  "`R/03_firstorder.R`", "quadrats, bandwidths, KDE, FRP, temporal", "`firstorder.rds`",
  "`R/04_secondorder.R`", "G, F, L, pcf, inhomogeneous versions, global tests", "`secondorder.rds`",
  "`R/05_spacetime.R`", "Knox test, relative risk, trajectory, space-time KDE", "`spacetime.rds`",
  "`R/06_covariates_models.R`", "OSM covariates from the Geofabrik extract, ppm, AIC, residual K, scan test", "`covariates_models.rds`",
  "`R/07_cluster_scale.R`", "Thomas process by explicit minimum contrast, with and without the trend", "`thomas.rds`",
  "`R/08_extended_range.R`", "second-order statistics to a 20 km lag, plus a correction cross-check", "`extended.rds`",
  "`R/helpers.R`", "one theme and one palette for every figure", "sourced by report and slides"
) |> kable()
```

The random seed is fixed at `r SEED` in `R/00_config.R` and set at the top of every
analysis script, so all Monte Carlo results reproduce exactly.

One engineering note that affects reproducibility in practice. `spatstat`'s `fv` and
`envelope` objects retain the closures used to construct them, and those closures
capture the calling environment. Because the analysis scripts hold several
multi-megabyte caches in that environment, saving the objects directly produced an
843 MB file for `extended.rds` alone. Each cache is therefore converted to plain
data frames before saving, which preserves every number and reduces the same file to
under a megabyte. The
geoBoundaries download is pinned to commit `9469f09` rather than to a moving
`current` endpoint. The FIRMS key is read from `.Renviron`, which is
git-ignored; `.Renviron.example` documents what is required.

```{r tbl-session}
#| label: tbl-session
#| tbl-cap: "Environment at render time."
si <- sessionInfo()
tibble::tibble(
  Component = c("R", "platform", "sf", "GDAL", "PROJ", "spatstat.explore",
                "spatstat.model", "ggplot2"),
  Version = c(paste(si$R.version$major, si$R.version$minor, sep = "."),
              si$platform, as.character(packageVersion("sf")),
              sf_extSoftVersion()[["GDAL"]], sf_extSoftVersion()[["PROJ"]],
              as.character(packageVersion("spatstat.explore")),
              as.character(packageVersion("spatstat.model")),
              as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")))) |> kable(align = "ll")
```
